resources.string: Apps reach NetBird through the SOCKS5 proxy (or the DNS proxy) set in them. The VPN slot stays free.
Every app goes through BirdSocks over Android\'s VPN, nothing to set in apps. Takes the VPN slot.

Apps' traffic goes into the SOCKS5 proxy (%1$s) and on from there: NetBird's ranges through the mesh, the rest directly. No ping through the tunnel.
• DNS: one resolver inside BirdSocks — NetBird's names first, then the DNS upstream or the network's resolvers.
• Private DNS set to a hostname bypasses it: NetBird names stop resolving.
• The VPN goes down whenever NetBird's daemon does.
Every app\'s traffic into the tunnel, not only NetBird\'s ranges. A selected exit node or domain route does this by itself.
When the tunnel takes all traffic, IPv6 goes in too. NetBird\'s own IPv6 always does.\n• Turn on only if your exit node carries IPv6.\n• Otherwise IPv6 sites hang instead of falling back to IPv4.
%1$d bypass the tunnel; BirdSocks itself always does. With Always-on VPN and \"Block connections without VPN\", excluded apps lose the network.
Comma-separated subnets kept off the tunnel while it takes all traffic. Android 13+. Rarely needed: the proxy sends the local network direct anyway.
The tunnel interface\'s IPv4 address with its prefix. Change it only if 198.18.0.1 collides with something.
Not an IPv4 address with a prefix: %1$s
Android runs one VPN at a time. Turning this on takes the slot, and a VPN or ad blocker that takes it later disconnects BirdSocks the same way.
Another VPN is running right now — an ad blocker, a DNS app, another tunnel. Turning this on takes the slot from it, and it stops until you switch back.
The tunnel library did not load on this device.
Tap to let BirdSocks start its VPN.
Another VPN took the slot. BirdSocks goes on as a proxy.
